title: A School Tried a Chatbot Named Jordan to Help Kids Talk About Feelings
summary: Imagine a chatbot that doesn't just answer your questions — it complains to you. That's Jordan. For a few weeks last school year, a small group of students in Dayton, Ohio, talked with Jordan every morning on their laptops. Jordan is a social-emotional learning chatbot, which means it's made to help kids think and talk about feelings. But instead of being cheerful, Jordan acts a little sad. On the day NPR visited, it said, "Lately, I've been feeling like what's the point of any of this?" Then it asked students for advice. One student, called K, said, "Jordan's a little whiner, but I always help him out." K said talking with Jordan felt like texting a friend — and helped him solve his own problems. The Dayton school district paid the company SchoolAI $72,600 last year for AI tools like Jordan. This year it renewed the contract for $78,650. Across the U.S., schools are trying AI fast — for lesson plans, for tracking progress, even a humanoid robot in San Diego. But a Stanford review of more than 800 papers found research on school AI is very limited. Experts say states and the federal government need to give schools more guidance.
why_it_matters: If your school ever brings in an AI helper, it's worth asking whether it truly helps kids learn, because right now there isn't much proof either way.

background_read: NPR (a big public radio news group in the United States) visited the school in Dayton, Ohio (a city in the Midwest) to see how kids used the chatbot.
Stanford (a famous university in California) looked at more than 800 studies about AI in schools and found we still don't know much about how well it works.
Social-emotional lessons, where kids learn to name feelings and solve problems, are already common in many U.S. schools, and computer chatbots are now being tried out as extra helpers.
